metadata.title: Stellate ganglion block associated with changes in depression and anxiety in idiopathic sudden sensorineural hearing loss: A retrospective observational study

sections.text: Idiopathic sudden sensorineural hearing loss (ISSNHL) is often accompanied by depression and anxiety. Stellate ganglion block (SGB) is useful to treat ISSNHL by enhancing cochlear perfusion. Recently, SGB has been reported to improve depressive symptoms in posttraumatic stress disorder, but it remains unclear whether SGB can decrease depressive symptoms and anxiety in patients with ISSNHL. In this single-center retrospective observational study, 35 patients with ISSNHL were included. Patients were treated with dexamethasone, low-molecular-weight dextran, and SGB. Depressive and anxiety symptoms were assessed using the Beck depression inventory (BDI) and generalized anxiety disorder-7 (GAD-7) before treatment (baseline), 1 hour after the 1st SGB (1 H) and 30 days after treatment (30D). Auditory function was evaluated by pure-tone audiometry (PTA) before and 30 days after treatment. PTA threshold significantly improved at 30D (47.9 ± 27.7), compared to baseline (68.0 ± 23.2) ( P < .001). The BDI significantly decreased at 1 H (5.5 ± 8.0) and 30D (4.5 ± 7.4), compared to baseline (9.1 ± 8.2) ( P < .0001). The GAD-7 significantly decreased at 1 H (2.3 ± 3.0) and Day 30 (1.9 ± 2.6), compared to baseline (4.7 ± 3.6) ( P < .0001). However, improvement in PTA is not correlated with improvement in BDI or GAD-7. SGB was associated with significant decreases in depressive and anxiety symptoms in patients with ISSNHL, which were not correlated with hearing recovery. These findings suggest that SGB may provide a potential benefit for mood improvement, independent of its effect on hearing recovery in this population.

Stellate ganglion block (SGB) is a percutaneous procedure in which a local anesthetic is administrated adjacent to the stellate ganglion to modulate sympathetic nervous system activity. [ 1 , 2 ] Clinically, it is used for patients with sympathetically mediated pain conditions, including complex regional pain syndrome and postherpetic neuralgia. [ 3 , 4 ] In addition, SGB has been used as an adjunctive therapy for various non-pain-related disorders including arrhythmias, lymphedema, idiopathic sudden sensorineural hearing loss (ISSNHL), and psychiatric disorders. [ 5 – 8 ] ISSNHL is classically defined as a hearing loss of 30 dB or worse in at least 3 contiguous frequencies within 72 hours. In 90% of cases the etiology is unknown. Proposed mechanisms of ISSNHL include viral infection, autoimmune inner-ear disease, and vascular insults. [ 9 ] ISSNHL is considered as an otologic emergency requiring early treatment, ideally within 14 days of symptom onset. [ 9 , 10 ] The primary treatment of ISSNHL is corticosteroid which can be administered systemically or via intratympanic injection. [ 11 , 12 ] Along with steroids, SGB is used as an adjunct treatment to enhance cochlear perfusion which can improve hearing recovery rates in patients with ISSNHL. [ 7 , 10 ] In addition, low-molecular-weight dextran or prostaglandin can be used to decrease inner ear hypoxia in ISSNHL. [ 13 ] Patients with ISSNHL have an increased risk of developing affective disorders such as depression and anxiety. ISSNHL impairs social communication, which leads to social isolation and contributes to onset of stress and depression. [ 14 , 15 ] Recently, SGB has been reported to be effective in alleviating anxiety and depressive symptoms in patients with posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD), and postpartum depression. [ 2 , 8 , 16 ] SGB is used as an adjunctive therapy for hearing recovery in ISSNHL. However, it remains unclear whether SGB can decrease depressive symptoms and anxiety in patients with ISSNHL. Therefore, this study aimed to investigate whether SGB improves depressive and anxiety symptoms in patients with ISSNHL.

This retrospective observational study was conducted at Kyungpook National University Hospital to evaluate the effects of SGB on depression and anxiety symptoms in patients with ISSNHL between January 2020 and December 2023. Patients with a history of diabetes mellitus, and psychological disorders were excluded. This study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and approved by the Institutional Review Board of Kyungpook National University Hospital (KNUH 2025-01-018). The requirement for informed consent was waived by the Institutional Review Board due to the retrospective nature of the study.

All patients with ISSNHL were treated within 7 days after onset of symptoms. Patients received intravenous dexamethasone 10 mg once daily for 5 days, followed by 5 mg once daily for 5 additional days. Additionally, intravenous low-molecular-weight dextran was administered for 10 consecutive days (Fig. 1 ). SGB with 5 mL of 1% lidocaine solution was performed at 3 hours before injection of dexamethasone under ultrasound guidance by an anesthesiologist. Patients received SGB every other day for 10 days (Fig. 1 ). Success of SGB was confirmed by the presence of ipsilateral Horner syndrome.

Auditory function was assessed by pure-tone audiometry (PTA), expressed as the average thresholds at 0.5, 1, and 2 kHz, and hearing outcomes were evaluated before treatment and 30 days after treatment (30D). Psychological symptoms were assessed using the Beck depression inventory (BDI) and the generalized anxiety disorder-7 (GAD-7) at baseline, 1 hour after the 1st SGB (1H) and 30D. The 1H time point was specifically chosen to capture the immediate sympatholytic and sedative effects of the procedure, as a demonstrated in our previous research. [ 17 ] Furthermore, because systemic dexamethasone was scheduled to be administered 3 hours after the SGB, assessing psychological outcomes at 1 hour allowed us to isolate the pure acute effects of SGB from any potential steroid-induced mood alterations. The questionnaires were completed by the patients in a supervised manner. A trained clinical nurse or physicians was present to provide standardized instructions, offer necessary assistance to prevent any distress, panic, or communication difficulties caused by the sudden hearing loss, and ensure the accurate and complete recording of the responses. The primary outcome was the change in BDI scores from baseline to 30D. The secondary outcome was the change in GAD-7 scores from baseline to 30D (Fig. 1 ).

Data were summarized with descriptive statistics. Correlations among PTA, BDI, and GAD-7 were assessed at baseline using Spearman rank analysis. Change in PTA from baseline to 30D was tested with a paired t test; when the normality assumption for paired differences failed on the Shapiro–Wilk test, the Wilcoxon signed rank test was used. Repeated measures of BDI and GAD-7 at baseline, 1H, and 30D were analyzed with a linear mixed-effects model including time as a fixed effect and subjects as a random effect. In accordance with the STROBE guidelines regarding the handling of missing data, a complete-case analysis approach was utilized; patients with incomplete clinical records or missing data for any of required outcomes at the designated time points were excluded during the initial screening phase. Correlations between changes from baseline to 30D in PTA and in BDI/GAD-7 were assessed with Spearman correlation. Analyses were performed in R, version 4.4.1 (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria) and a P -value of <.05 was considered statistically significant.

sections.section: 3.1. Demographic Data And Correlations Of Baseline Parameters
sections.text: A total of 35 patients were enrolled for the study. There were no missing data in the final cohort of the patients. The demographic data and clinical characteristics are shown in Table 1 .
PTA thresholds were significantly improved at 30D (47.9 ± 27.7), compared to baseline (68.0 ± 23.2) ( P < .001) (Fig. 2 ).

BDI significantly decreased at 1H (5.5 ± 8.0) and 30D (4.5 ± 7.4), compared to baseline (9.1 ± 8.2) ( P < .0001, respectively). However, there was no significant difference between 1H and 30D ( P = .13) (Fig. 3 ). SGB was effective in decreasing depressive symptom in patients with ISSNHL. At baseline,6 patients (17.1%) exhibited depressive symptoms of at least mild severity (BDI ≥ 13, which is consistent with the optimal screening threshold for nonpsychiatric settings). [ 18 ] At 30 days, the prevalence of depressive symptoms significantly decreased to 1 patient (2.9%).

GAD-7 scores significantly decreased at 1H (2.3 ± 3.0) and at 30D (1.9 ± 2.6), compared with baseline (4.7 ± 3.6) ( P < .0001, respectively). However, there was no significant difference between 1H and 30D ( P = .40) (Fig. 4 ). At baseline, 10 patients (28.6%) presented with GAD-7 scores ≥5 (indicating at least mild anxiety). [ 19 ] Following treatment, only 4 patients (11.4%) remained in the symptomatic range at 30 days. SGB was effective in decreasing anxiety in patients with ISSHL.

sections.section: 3.5. Correlations Among Pta, Bdi, And Gad-7
sections.text: Improvement in PTA was not significantly associated with improvement in BDI ( R = 0.149, P = .393) or improvement in GAD-7 ( R = 0.041, P = .813), respectively. However, there was a significant positive correlation between BDI improvement and GAD-7 improvement at 1H (Spearman ρ = 0.40, P = .018) and at 30D (ρ = 0.47, P = .004).

In this study, we investigated the effects of SGB on depressive and anxiety symptoms in patients with ISSNHL. BDI and GAD-7 scores are useful to evaluate the degree of depression and anxiety. [ 20 ] Our findings demonstrate that adjunctive SGB was associated with significant and rapid reductions in both BDI and GAD-7 scores at 1 hour posttreatment, which were maintained at 30 days. Furthermore, while auditory function (PTA) also significantly improved over the 30-day period, the improvements in mood symptoms were statistically independent of the degree of hearing recovery. Conversely, BDI improvement was positively associated with GAD-7 improvement at both follow-up points. Regarding clinical relevance, the improvements observed in our study exceeded established minimal clinically important differences (MCIDs). The 4.6-point (50.5%) reduction in mean BID scores robustly surpassed the established BDI MCIDs of 3.5 points or a 17.5% reduction. [ 21 , 22 ] For the GAD-7, while the absolute reduction of 2.8 points was contrained by a floor effect against the generic 4-point MCID used for severe cohorts, it clearly exceeded the baseline-dependent MCID of 1.5 points (or 20% relative reduction) for mild-symptom cohorts as well as the universally accepted distribution-based MCID of 1.8 points (half of the standard deviation). This indicates that the statistically significant findings translate to clinically meaningful symptom relief. [ 22 – 24 ] ISSNHL severely decreases patient’s quality of life and creates stress by affecting social communication. [ 14 , 15 ] It was demonstrated that stress-induced neuroinflammation contributes to the pathogenesis of mood disorders such as depression and anxiety. In animal models and populations with severe neuropsychiatric conditions, stress triggers alterations in brain oxygen metabolism and leads to mitochondrial dysfunction, which activates NF-κB signaling and the HIF-1α/NLRP3 inflammasome, resulting in progression of mental health conditions such as depression and anxiety. [ 25 , 26 ] In addition, stress induces dysregulation of sympathetic nerve system and dysfunction of hypothalamic pituitary adrenal axis, which leads to development of depression and anxiety disorders. [ 27 – 30 ] SGB involves the injection of a local anesthetic adjacent to the stellate ganglion, a sympathetic ganglion that mediates the “fight-or-flight” response. [ 31 ] It was shown that SGB induces sedative effects in the animal study [ 32 ] and human study. [ 17 ] The previous studies demonstrated that SGB suppresses HIF-1α/NLRP3 and NF-κB activity, leading to a significant improvement of affective disorders. [ 33 , 34 ] In addition, SGB attenuates the autonomic imbalance and stabilizes dysfunction of the neuroendocrine system in mental disorders. [ 35 ] Because our study relied soley on self-reported clinical scales without measuring specific biomarkers, we cannot directly confirm the modulation of these pathways in our cohort. Therefore, our discussing liking SGB to the modulation of sympathetic tone, hypothalamic pituitary adrenal axis regulation, and the suppression of specific molecular pathways should be viewed as extrapolations and hypothesis-generating mechanistic speculations rather than inferred effects directly supported by our data. In the present study, there is no significant difference between right- and left-sided SGB effect on changes in BDI and GAD-7. Regarding autonomic asymmetry and lateralization effects, the right hemisphere of the brain has a more significant involvement in the human stress response. [ 36 ] Therefore, the right-sided SGB was commonly performed in patients with psychiatric disorder. [ 8 ] However, left-sided SGB led to a significant improvement in patients with PTSD who did not respond to right sided SGB. [ 37 ] It was suggested that patients who responded to a left (but not right-sided SGB have anatomical differences requiring contralateral rather than ipsilateral intervention). [ 37 ] Horner syndrome is a reliable indicator of a successful SGB. Ultrasound guided SGB increases the safety and success rate of the procedure, compared with blind technique. [ 38 ] In this study, ultrasound guided SGB were performed every other day over 10 days and all patients exhibited ipsilateral Horner syndrome after procedure. In a previous randomized clinical trial, 2 SGB treatments administered 2 weeks apart significantly reduced PTSD symptom severity over 8 weeks. [ 16 ] In the present study, the values of BDI and GAD-7 significantly decreased at 1 hour after the 1st SGB, which last after 30 days after intervention. Although the fundamental neurobiological resolution of depression typically requires a longer duration, the significant improvement in BDI and GAD-7 scores observed at 1hour post-SGB may be attributed to the acute sympatholytic effects of the procedure. By blocking sympathetic hyperactivity, SGB can provide immediate relief of the somatic symptoms of anxiety and stress, which likely contributed to the reduction in self-reported symptom scores. [ 39 , 40 ] SGB has been shown to be effective in treating symptoms of PTSD and anxiety in previous clinical trials, with results seen over a period of weeks. [ 16 , 41 ] However, few studies have quantified the immediate psychological response. In the present study, the significant reduction in BDI and GAD-7 scores as early as 1-hour post-SGB aligns with the procedure’s rapid physiological mechanism. Our previous research has shown that SGB induces immediate sedation and reduces sympathetic outflow, as evidence by a decrease in the Bispectral Index. [ 17 ] We propose that the rapid improvement in mood scores at 1 hour after treatment reflects this acute alleviation of somatic anxiety and tension, distinct from the longer-term effect on mood symptoms. A potential confounder in this study is the concurrent improvement in hearing, which could naturally alleviate psychological distress. However, several findings suggest an independent effect of SGB. First, we observed significant mood improvement as early as 1 hour after SGB. According to the natural history of ISSNHL, hearing recovery is a gradual process that typically begins around Day 3 of treatment and proceeds over the 1st week. [ 42 ] Therefore, the rapid reduction in BDI and GAD-7 scores at 1 hour is unlikely to be a secondary reaction to restored hearing. Second, the lack of statistical correlation between PTA improvement and mood scores at 30 days further supports the hypothesis that SGB exerts a direct mood-modulating effect, independent of auditor outcomes. In the present study, PTA values greatly improved at 30 days after treatments including steroid, dextran, and SGB. However, there was no significant relation between degree of PTA reduction and degree of improvement of depression and anxiety. Therefore, SGB may provide a beneficial effect for improvement of mood symptoms in patients with ISSNHL, independent of its effect on hearing recovery. Steroids can induce mood changes such as euphoria, anxiety, and depression. The psychiatric adverse effects usually appear within the few days or weeks after treatment of steroid. [ 43 ] In this study, the 1st SGB was performed before administration of steroid and psychological symptoms were greatly improved 1 hour after the intervention. However, there was no difference between 1 hour and 30 days after SGB. The previous study showed the PTSD greatly improved within 5 minutes of SGB, which lasted 1 month or longer. [ 39 ] Therefore, it was presumed that SGB reduced depression and anxiety symptoms in patients with ISSNHL.

Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, the retrospective, uncontrolled single-center design limits causal inference. The observed improvements in mood may reflect regression to the mean, placebo effects, natural psychological adaptation to the acute illness, or the relief associated with engagement in active treatment, rather than a direct specific efficacy of SGB. In addition, the small sample size of the study may limit the ability to extrapolate the results beyond the studied population. Second, psychological assessments were limited to self-reported questionnaires without clinician-administered scales. Third, the lack of a control group precludes direct causal inference. Future prospective controlled studies with larger cohorts and longer follow-up are warranted.

SGB significantly decreases depressive and anxiety symptoms in patients with ISSNHL, independent of its effect on hearing improvement. These findings suggest that SGB may offer a therapeutic option for management of mood symptoms in this population.
